gloss_terse: Conditional particle: if, or, whether; also concessive (though) and asseverative (surely) in oaths
gloss_readable: One of the most versatile logical connectors in Biblical Hebrew, 'im functions primarily as the conditional 'if' that introduces nearly every protasis in the Old Testament. Beyond conditionality, it branches into disjunction ('or,' especially in paired 'im...'im constructions), indirect questions ('whether'), and even rhetorical force. In oath formulas it carries an implicit negation — 'if I do this' meaning 'I surely will not' — a usage preserved in Arabic 'in and Aramaic 'en. Its 922 occurrences touch virtually every genre of biblical prose and poetry.

senses.1: The dominant conditional use (827x), introducing protases with imperfect or perfect verbs. Spanish si, French si, and German wenn/ob all converge on the conditional reading. Key passages like Gen 4:7 ('if you do well') and Gen 13:16 ('if one could count the dust') show both real and hypothetical conditions. The cross-linguistic uniformity here confirms a single stable sense.
senses.2: Disjunctive 'or' (82x), presenting alternatives or choices. German oder and Spanish o clearly mark this as distinct from the conditional. Paired constructions 'im...'im ('whether...or') appear in Gen 24:21 and Gen 37:32, where the speaker poses two possibilities. The Arabic cognate 'am similarly serves as a disjunctive particle, confirming the Semitic pedigree of this usage.
senses.3: Indirect-question 'whether' (8x), introducing uncertainty after verbs of knowing or testing. German ob and Spanish si capture this epistemic nuance well. Exod 19:13 and Lev 27:26 show contexts where the outcome is genuinely unknown to the speaker. This overlaps with the conditional but is syntactically distinct in embedding under cognitive verbs.
senses.4: Rhetorical interrogative marker (3x), expecting a strong affirmative or negative answer. The glosses 'indeed' and 'is it not?' reflect this force. Num 17:13 and Job 6:13 show the particle pressing the hearer toward an obvious conclusion, a pragmatic extension of the conditional into discourse-level persuasion.
senses.5: Concessive 'though' or 'even if' (1x at 1Sam 15:17), where the condition is granted rather than questioned. Samuel's rebuke 'though you are small in your own eyes' acknowledges the premise while overriding it. This rare use parallels Arabic 'in with concessive force in classical rhetoric.
senses.6: Asseverative 'surely' in oath formulas (1x at Gen 15:4), where 'im carries implicit self-imprecation: 'if I do X [may God punish me],' meaning 'I surely will not.' German nur ('only') and Spanish que hint at the restrictive-emphatic flavor. This idiomatic oath usage is well attested across Semitic languages.

gloss_terse: Soul, life, self, person; the breathing inner being — seat of desire, emotion, and vital existence
gloss_readable: Perhaps the richest anthropological term in the Hebrew Bible, nephesh encompasses the entire animated person — from the breath of life God breathed into Adam (Gen 2:7) to the desperate cry 'my soul thirsts for God' (Ps 42:2). It resists neat translation: Korean splits it between 영혼 ('soul') and 생명 ('life'), Swahili between nafsi ('inner self') and uhai ('vitality'), and Spanish between alma and vida. In legal texts it simply means 'person' — a counted head. At its root, nephesh is whatever makes a creature alive, wanting, and present in the world.

senses.1: The immaterial inner self or soul (647x) — the seat of emotions, will, and spiritual life. Korean 영혼 and Swahili nafsi consistently mark this core sense. Gen 49:6 ('let my soul not enter their council') and Ps 42:1 show nephesh as the conscious, feeling self that relates to God and others. This is the dominant sense across nearly all genres.
senses.2: Physical life or vital existence (94x) that can be risked, lost, or saved. Korean 생명/목숨 and Swahili uhai/maisha distinguish this from the inner-self sense. Exod 21:23 ('life for life') and Exod 4:19 ('those who sought your life') show nephesh as the stake in mortal danger — something concretely at risk rather than an interior state.
senses.3: Desire, appetite, or volitional craving (9x). Korean 소원/뜻 and Swahili tamaa/hamu isolate this appetitive meaning. Gen 23:8 ('if it is your desire') and Deut 23:24 ('eat grapes to your desire') show nephesh as the wanting faculty — what the self reaches for, whether food, possession, or a loved one (Gen 34:3, 8).
senses.4: A person or individual as a countable unit (5x), especially in legal and census contexts. Korean 사람 and Spanish persona mark this impersonal usage. Lev 27:2 ('the valuation of persons') and Deut 24:7 ('kidnapping a person') treat nephesh as a human head to be enumerated or legislated about, stripped of its emotive connotations.
senses.5: Breath or life-breath (1x at Job 41:21), describing the fiery exhalation of Leviathan. English 'his breath' and Spanish 'su aliento' capture the physical respiratory image. This rare usage preserves the etymological link between nephesh and naphash ('to breathe'), grounding the abstract soul-concept in concrete respiration.
senses.6: The animating principle that constitutes a living being (1x at Gen 2:7), where God breathes into Adam and he becomes a 'living nephesh.' French dans-âme and German zu-einer-Seele point to the transformative moment: not a soul entering a body, but dust becoming an ensouled creature. This foundational verse anchors the entire semantic range.

gloss_terse: Call, summon, name; cry out in distress; proclaim publicly; read aloud; invite to a gathering
gloss_readable: A foundational verb of vocal action in Biblical Hebrew, qara' covers the full spectrum from naming a child (Gen 2:19) to crying out to God in anguish (Judg 15:18) to reading the Torah scroll aloud before the assembly (Deut 31:11). Arabic preserves a revealing split: da'a covers calling and summoning while qara'a specializes in reading and recitation — the very root that gives us 'Qur'an.' Korean similarly distinguishes 부르다 (call/name) from 읽다 (read) and 부르짖다 (cry out), confirming that these are genuinely distinct senses within a single lexeme.

senses.1: The core sense of calling, summoning, or naming (575x). Arabic da'a, Korean 부르다, and Swahili kuita all converge here. Gen 2:19 (Adam naming animals), Gen 22:11 (the angel calling Abraham), and Gen 20:8 (Abimelech summoning servants) illustrate the breadth — from bestowing identity to commanding attention. This is the semantic center from which all other senses radiate.
senses.2: Crying out in distress or urgent appeal (69x). Korean 부르짖다/외치다 and Spanish clamar/gritar distinguish this from neutral calling. Judg 15:18 (Samson crying out in thirst) and Judg 16:28 (his final prayer) show the desperate vocal quality. Swahili kupiga kelele ('make a commotion') captures the intensity. The cry is typically directed upward — to God — or outward in alarm.
senses.3: Formal public proclamation or announcement (32x). Korean 선포하다 and Swahili kutangaza mark the official, authoritative register. Exod 33:19 and 34:5-6 (God proclaiming his own name and attributes) show the theological weight this sense carries. Lev 23:2 (proclaiming sacred assemblies) illustrates its ritual-administrative function in Israelite life.
senses.4: Passive: to be called or named (Nifal/Pual, 30x). Arabic du'iya, Korean 불리다, and Swahili -itwa consistently render the passive voice. Gen 48:6 ('they shall be called by the name of their brothers') and Deut 28:10 ('all peoples shall see that you are called by the name of the LORD') show naming as identity-conferral from outside the individual.
senses.5: Reading a written text aloud or reciting from a scroll (24x). Arabic qara'a — the root of 'Qur'an' — preserves this specific meaning. Korean 읽다 and Swahili kusoma ('study/read') distinguish it from oral calling. Exod 24:7 (Moses reading the Book of the Covenant), Deut 17:19, and Josh 8:34 (Joshua reading the Torah) show this as a public liturgical act.
senses.6: Inviting or summoning to a feast, sacrifice, or social gathering (9x). Arabic mad'uww ('invited one') and Korean 초대하다 ('invite') isolate this social-hospitality sense. Exod 34:15 (being invited to eat idol sacrifices) and 1Sam 9:13, 22, 24 (Samuel inviting Saul to the sacrificial banquet) show the verb in convivial contexts where the calling is to shared food and fellowship.

gloss_terse: Have, possess; hold fast; be in a state; be pregnant; regard as; neighboring (middle participle)
gloss_readable: The Greek verb echo is among the most frequent in the New Testament, appearing over 700 times. At its core it means 'to have' or 'to possess,' but its semantic reach extends far beyond ownership. Combined with adverbs it becomes quasi-copular ('kalos echo' = 'I am well'), with 'en gastri' it means 'to be pregnant,' and in the middle participle echomenos it means 'next' or 'neighboring.' Spanish distinguishes tener (possess) from estar (be in a state), neatly separating the two largest senses. This versatility makes echo one of the workhorses of koine Greek grammar.

senses.1: General possession or having (680x) — the overwhelming default sense. Spanish tiene, French avoir, and German haben all map here without ambiguity. Matt 8:20 ('the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head') and Matt 13:12 ('whoever has, to him more will be given') show echo in its most basic possessive function, covering material goods, qualities, relationships, and abstract attributes alike.
senses.2: Quasi-copular 'to be in a state' (9x), where echo plus an adverb expresses condition rather than possession. Spanish estar (not tener) signals this shift clearly. Mark 2:17 ('those who are sick,' kakos echontes) and Mark 5:23 ('my daughter is at the point of death,' eschatos echei) show the verb functioning as 'to be' with an adverbial complement — a well-documented koine Greek idiom.
senses.3: Idiomatic 'to be pregnant' (en gastri echo, 7x), a fixed collocation meaning 'to have in the womb.' Matt 1:18 (Mary 'was found to be with child') and Matt 24:19 ('woe to those who are pregnant') use this phrase. Spanish que tiene(n) and German haben preserve the literal 'have' construction, while the context makes the specialized meaning unmistakable.
senses.4: To hold, grasp, or hold fast (6x), emphasizing retention or physical grip rather than static possession. Mark 16:8 ('trembling and astonishment held them') and 1Tim 3:9 ('holding the mystery of the faith') show both literal and metaphorical gripping. Spanish ten (imperative 'hold!') and the participial 'holding' in multiple languages distinguish this active, volitional sense.
senses.5: To regard as or consider (5x), where echo takes a double accusative or predicate complement. Matt 14:5 ('he held him as a prophet') and Matt 21:26 ('they all hold John as a prophet') show estimation rather than possession. Spanish lo tenian ('they regarded him') preserves the same construction. Phil 2:29 ('hold such people in honor') extends this into ethical exhortation.
senses.6: Middle participle echomenos meaning 'next, adjoining, neighboring' (4x). Spanish siguiente/cercanas and German-based glosses mark the spatial or temporal adjacency. Mark 1:38 ('let us go to the neighboring towns'), Luke 13:33 ('the next day'), and Acts 20:15 show this specialized participial form functioning as an adjective entirely detached from the verb's possessive core.
